an1.188:1.1: Koṇḍañña gained his nickname as he was the first person to realize the Dhamma after the Buddha ([sn56.11:14.3]()). His absence was due to his love of solitude, as expressed in his verses ([thag15.1:0.4]()). Due to this, he features rarely in the early texts, but the Buddha once saw him meditating ([ud7.6]()), and he once came to show extreme devotion to the Buddha ([sn8.9[()).
an1.189:1.1: Sāriputta, also called Upatissa, became a stream-enterer on hearing a short teaching from the monk Assaji ([pli-tv-kd1:23.5.6]()), whereupon he told his friend Moggallāna. They both promptly left their former teacher Sañjaya, a traumatic loss to Sañjaya and his community. [an4.172:2.1]() says that Sāriputta became enlightened a fortnight after he ordained, a detail confirmed in multiple parallels to this passage; [mn111:2.8]() details the practice he undertook in that fortnight. The Suttas feature his teachings extensively, but his detailed analytical style is best exemplified in such texts as [mn9](), [mn28](), and [mn140](). He is remembered in the tradition for his warmth and dignity of character. He passed away shortly before the Buddha ([sn47.13]()).
an1.190:1.1: Mahāmoggallāna (or simply Moggallāna; also called Kolita), displays his spectacular mastery of psychic powers in such texts as [mn37](), but also taught on the details of ethical conduct ([mn15]()), or conversed with Sāriputta on the motivations for misconduct ([mn5]()). After going forth with Sāriputta, he was advised by the Buddha on meditation ([an7.61]()). Like Sāriputta, he pre-deceased the Buddha ([sn47.14]()), but the circumstances of his death are not recorded, and later accounts are not reliable.
an1.191:1.1: Mahākassapa was the former husband of Bhaddā Kāpilānī ([an1.244]()). He was known for his simple and austere lifestyle, devotion to the Buddha, support for the poor ([ud1.6]()), and love of nature. He was the senior disciple to survive the Buddha ([dn16:6.19.1]()), and presided over the First Council ([pli-tv-kd21]()). His death is not recorded in early texts, and legend says he is still alive, meditating in a mountain cave where he awaits the next Buddha, to whom he will present his robe as an offering.
